title: RNA-Based Therapies for Lipoprotein(a) Reduction: Antisense Oligonucleotides, Small Interfering RNAs, and Emerging Platforms.
authors: ['Vibhu Parcha', 'Vera A Bittner']
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent, genetically determined, and causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) and calcific aortic valve stenosis. Elevated Lp(a) affects approximately 20% of the global population and is not meaningfully modified by lifestyle intervention or existing lipid-lowering pharmacotherapy. This review summarizes the biology of Lp(a) as a therapeutic target, evaluates the efficacy of currently available lipid-lowering agents against this target, and describes the mechanistic principles, clinical evidence, and unresolved questions associated with RNA-based and emerging small-molecule and gene-editing approaches to Lp(a) reduction. RECENT FINDINGS: Four RNA-directed agents targeting hepatic apolipoprotein(a) [apo(a)] synthesis have entered phase 2/3 development. This includes pelacarsen, an antisense oligonucleotide (ASO), and olpasiran, zerlasiran, and lepodisiran, which are N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated small interfering RNAs (siRNAs). Phase 2 data demonstrate Lp(a) reductions ranging from 79% to approximately 97% on a placebo-adjusted basis, approaching the practical limit of apo(a) suppression, with favorable short-term safety profiles. A fifth, structurally distinct siRNA conjugated with GalNAc at both strand termini has recently completed first-in-human testing, sustaining reductions up to 97% through 48 weeks after a single dose without injection-site reactions. Recently, the topline results of phase 3 Lp(a) HORIZON (pelacarsen) were released and demonstrate a substantial Lp(a) reduction without meeting the trial's primary composite cardiovascular endpoint. Two further outcomes trials, OCEAN(a)-Outcomes (olpasiran) and ACCLAIM-Lp(a) (lepodisiran), remain ongoing. An oral small molecule, muvalaplin, achieved comparable reductions in phase 2 testing. Lastly, early non-human primate data, together with a completed phase 1 trial of an analogous CRISPR-Cas9 construct targeting a related hepatic lipid gene, support the feasibility of a CRISPR-Cas9-based gene-editing approach capable of durable apo(a) suppression from a single administration. The pharmacology of Lp(a) suppression is now well characterized across three distinct therapeutic modalities. Whether the magnitude of biochemical reduction observed translates into a meaningful and safe reduction in cardiovascular events across different populations remains undetermined and will be addressed by the ongoing outcomes trials.
keywords: ['Antisense oligonucleotide', 'Cardiovascular disease', 'Gene editing', 'Lipoprotein(a)', 'RNAi therapeutics', 'Small interfering RNA']

title: Chemically composed Cas9 (ChemComCas9) for spatio-temporal regulation and precision genome engineering applications.
authors: ['Pallabi Das', 'Tuhin Baran Samoi', 'Basudeb Maji']
abstract: Chemically composed Cas9 (ChemComCas9) has emerged as a highly versatile CRISPR enzyme, offering tunable, on-demand, and targeted control over genome engineering functions. Despite its programmable, sequence-specific activity, uncontrolled or prolonged exposure to Cas9 can lead to severe genotoxicity, restricting its enormous clinical potential. To circumvent its non-specific and uncontrolled activities, Cas9 has been chemically modified for spatio-temporal and precision control. For developing such ChemComCas9, the WT Cas9 has been chemically modified using either its surface-exposed natural cysteine or by the installation of additional cysteine residues, or an unnatural amino acid has been incorporated for chemical modification. Such strategies include the incorporation of peptides, polymers, antibodies, stimuli-responsive moieties, and biorthogonal conjugation techniques that allow external control over Cas9 activation, localization, and activity. In addition, various short peptides have been either genetically fused or chemically conjugated for spatiotemporal regulation and probing. These approaches enable conditional activation of Cas9 in response to light, small molecules, or intracellular triggers, thereby minimizing off-target effects and increasing editing efficiency. In this review, we discuss a systematic evolution of chemically composed Cas9 (ChemComCas9) for precision genome engineering and gene therapy applications.

title: Interactive Media Engagement Predicts Posttraumatic Distress After Community Trauma: A National Repeated Cross-Sectional Study.
authors: ['Sun Wook Jung', 'Mi Yeon Lee', 'Kang-Seob Oh', 'Young-Chul Shin', 'Dong-Won Shin', 'Sang-Won Jeon', 'Junhyung Kim', 'Eun Soo Kim', 'Se Youl Kim', 'Kwang-Yeol Lee', 'Nahyun Oh', 'Sra Jung', 'Sung Joon Cho']
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Media engagement is an important pathway for indirect exposure to community trauma, but little is known about how interactive platforms and meaning-making relate to posttraumatic psychological outcomes. This study examined whether different types of media usage, particularly interactive online engagement, predict acute and subacute posttraumatic distress following a communitylevel traumatic event. METHODS: A two-wave nationwide repeated cross-sectional survey was conducted 2 weeks (n=1,703) and 2 months (n=2,220) post-incident, using stratified quota sampling. Depressive, anxiety, and posttraumatic stress (PTS) symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9, Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale, and the Posttraumatic Stress Disorder Checklist for the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition. Analyses included chi-square tests, analysis of covariance with Bonferroni correction, and multivariable regression models. RESULTS: Interactive engagement correlated with elevated psychological distress at both time points. At 2 months, receiving information through online communities and sharing graphic content predicted greater symptom severity and higher odds of clinically significant depressive, anxiety, and PTS symptoms. Passive exposure to graphics was not associated with elevated distress and was linked to lower symptom prevalence. Personal relevance to victims and systemic attribution were also significant predictors, with media types showing clearer differences at 2 months. CONCLUSION: Posttraumatic distress following community trauma appears to be shaped more by patterns of interaction with trauma-related information than by visual exposure. Interactive online engagement may amplify psychological symptoms over time, highlighting the need for public health strategies that address interactive media environments.

title: Personalizing digital mental health: a micro-randomized trial analysis of cognitive behavioral therapy/dialectical behavioral therapy text messages to improve mood.
authors: ['Caroline A Figueroa', 'Jing Xu', 'Marvyn R Arévalo Avalos', 'Bibhas Chakraborty', 'Adrian Aguilera']
abstract: PURPOSE: Digital mental health interventions could improve population health. However, our understanding of how to improve their effectiveness through personalization is limited. We describe the outcomes of a micro-randomized trial (MRT) of a 60-day text messaging program, delivered during the final stages of the COVID-19 pandemic. We analyze the effects of 6 different types of cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) messages, and examine whether socio-demographic, health-related, and contextual factors (eg, timing of sending a message) moderate effectiveness. METHODS: This secondary analysis included 373 adults aged 18 years or older (mean = 38.07), mostly English-speaking female, highly educated White individuals who reported being in good health, but having high stress and struggling to get their basic needs met. Participants were recruited between December 2021 and September 2022 through social media and a recruitment service (Health Match). We used the weighted and centered least squares method to examine the proximal effects of the text-message categories on daily mood, and whether sociodemographic, health-related factors, and the timing of message delivery moderated effectiveness. RESULTS: None of the 6 CBT/DBT-message categories significantly improved mood ratings marginally. However, their effectiveness varied based on the time of day and self-reported health. Overall, sending a message in the afternoon was more effective. However, certain message categories showed significant effects when sent in the morning among participants with poorer self-reported health, while some showed lower effectiveness when sent in the late afternoon for participants with better health. CONCLUSION: Our analysis underscores the importance of considering the time of day and individual health status when developing digital mental health interventions. These insights can help in designing more personalized, adaptive, and effective digital interventions.

title: AI representations of mental health stigma: Quantifying the gap between AI estimations and human perceptions across gender groups using GPT-based LLMs.
authors: ['Soojong Kim', 'Hye Min Kim', 'Kwanho Kim', 'Dongdong Zhu']
abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in mental health applications raises concerns about its potential to internalize and perpetuate societal biases. This research evaluates both disparities and misalignment in how large language models (LLMs), GPT-4 and GPT-5, represent perceptions of mental health across gender groups. The research comprises two studies. Study 1 applied widely adopted measures of Social Distance, Stereotypes, and Attitudes Toward Seeking Help to assess whether the AI models depict systematic gender differences. Study 2 compared AI estimations of Personal, Self, and Perceived Stigma with large-scale real-world human data from the Healthy Minds Study (N = 76,406) to evaluate alignment between AI estimations and human perceptions. Results from Study 1 showed the AI models consistently portrayed men as having the greatest desire for social distance from someone with mental health problems, relatively higher Stereotypes scores, and the least favorable attitudes toward help-seeking, compared with women and nonbinary individuals. Study 2 confirmed that this ordinal pattern partially aligned with human-reported data for Personal and Self Stigma. However, the AI models systematically underestimated Personal Stigma and Perceived Stigma while substantially overestimating Self Stigma for all gender groups. These findings reveal that, although the AI models have learned relative gender-based patterns reflecting human experiences to a certain extent, they function as distorted portrayals, highlighting the need for rigorous, context-specific validation against real-world data to ensure AI's safe and equitable deployment.

title: AI and analytics in sports: Leveraging BERTopic to map the past and chart the future
authors: ['Manit Mishra']
abstract: Purpose: The purpose of this study is to map the body of scholarly literature at the intersection of artificial intelligence (AI), analytics and sports and thereafter, leverage the insights generated to chart guideposts for future research. Design/methodology/approach: The study carries out systematic literature review (SLR). Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) protocol is leveraged to identify 204 journal articles pertaining to utilization of AI and analytics in sports published during 2002 to 2024. We follow it up with extraction of the latent topics from sampled articles by leveraging the topic modelling technique of BERTopic. Findings: The study identifies the following as predominant areas of extant research on usage of AI and analytics in sports: performance modelling, physical and mental health, social media sentiment analysis, and tactical tracking. Each extracted topic is further examined in terms of its relative prominence, representative studies, and key term associations. Drawing on these insights, the study delineates promising avenues for future inquiry. Research limitations/implications: The study offers insights to academicians and sports administrators on transformational impact of AI and analytics in sports. Originality/value: The study introduces BERTopic as a novel approach for extracting latent structures in sports research, thereby advancing both scholarly understanding and the methodological toolkit of the field.

title: Multiscale Water Balance Analysis and Water Network Resilience Optimization in the Yellow River Basin.
authors: ['Tao Du', 'Zhilei Yu', 'Dengming Yan', 'Ze Yuan', 'Zhong Lu', 'Yan Xu', 'Quanlai Ma', 'Chouke Yang']
abstract: As a core region for ecological security, food production, and energy supply in China, the hydrological cycle of the Yellow River Basin is being profoundly altered by climate change and intensive human activities, leading to growing systemic water scarcity and increasingly heterogeneous hydrological processes. However, the lack of long-term and high-resolution hydrological data has constrained the accurate characterization of multilayer water exchange processes among the atmosphere, surface water, and groundwater at the basin scale, thereby limiting the development of sustainable water resource management strategies. This study integrates multisource remote sensing data with hydrological models to reveal the spatiotemporal evolution of the basin water cycle and to develop a resilience-oriented water network for sustainable management. By integrating remote sensing products such as GRACE and ETMonitor with distributed hydrological models, the study systematically evaluated the multilevel water balance dynamics of the Yellow River Basin from atmospheric precipitation to groundwater storage during 1991-2020. The results show that the remotely sensed groundwater storage anomaly (GWSA) agrees well with in situ groundwater-level observations at the regional scale. The ETMonitor model performs well in estimating evapotranspiration over vegetated areas, with a validation root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.93 mm/day. The study revealed a pronounced spatiotemporal pattern of "water surplus in the west and water deficit in the east" across the Yellow River Basin, with the polarization intensifying under the combined effects of upstream climatic warming and humidification and intensive water consumption in the middle and lower reaches. Based on improved intelligent algorithms and channel topology constraints, this study proposed an optimized basin water network scheme. After optimization, the areal extent of water-deficient regions decreased substantially, water stress in the middle and lower reaches was alleviated, and both the balance and the efficiency of basin-wide water allocation improved. This research provides a quantitative basis for refined water resource management, water-saving irrigation retrofitting, and optimized planning of the national water network in the Yellow River Basin.

title: Recommendations for HIV care continuity during droughts and floods with key populations living with HIV in Kampala, Uganda: Qualitative insights.
authors: ['Carmen H Logie', 'Moses Okumu', 'Bay Bahri', 'Frannie MacKenzie', 'Gerald Pande', 'Brenda Katisi', 'Aidah Nakitende', 'Peter Kyambadde', 'Lawrence Mbuagbaw', 'Lesley Gittings', 'Caetano Dorea', 'Paul Bukuluki', 'Julien Brisson']
abstract: BackgroundClimate change and extreme weather events increasingly threaten HIV care continuity, yet evidence centering the lived experiences of key populations living with HIV remains limited. To address this knowledge gap, this qualitative study elicited recommendations for strengthening HIV service delivery during droughts and floods with young men who have sex with men (MSM) and female sex workers (FSW) living with HIV in Kampala, Uganda.MethodsThis community-based qualitative study involved semi-structured interviews with a purposive sample of young people (aged 18-24) living with HIV (8 MSM, 8 FSW) and 20 key informants from community leadership, climate, and HIV sectors from May-July 2024. Data were analyzed using framework thematic analysis and organized across institutional, community, and household level strategies.ResultsThe 36 participants included 16 people living with HIV (8 MSM, 8 FSW; median age 23.5) and 20 key informants (7 women, 13 men) representing community leadership (n = 4), climate and environmental issues (n = 8), and HIV expertise (n = 8). Participants identified multi-level and interconnected strategies to sustain HIV care during droughts and floods. Institutional-level recommendations included decentralizing and mobilizing antiretroviral therapy (ART) delivery, expanding multi-month dispensing, maintaining emergency drug buffers, integrating nutritional support to address food insecurity, and equipping frontline workers for adverse weather conditions. Community-level strategies emphasized livelihood and savings initiatives, environmental management, infrastructure improvements, peer support networks, and targeted outreach during weather-related disruptions. Household-level strategies included strengthening food and water security, diversifying income sources, planning ahead for treatment continuity, and using practical transport solutions, such as bicycles, to overcome flood-related barriers.ConclusionsSustaining HIV care during weather-related disruptions requires coordinated responses that extend beyond the health sector. Climate-resilient HIV programmes should integrate service delivery adaptations with social protection, livelihood support, infrastructure investments, and community-led interventions to enable uninterrupted HIV care for young Ugandan key populations with HIV in climate-affected settings.

title: CRISPR genome editing in food and feed crops: intellectual property challenges, global accessibility, and the Indian perspective.
authors: ['Harshit Mangal', 'Shivangi Mathur', 'Anurag Chaurasia', 'Soumya Sharma', 'Sunil Kumar', 'Rajiv Ranjan']
abstract: The ever-increasing global demand for food and feed, coupled with population growth and climate change, necessitates the development of high-yielding and stress-resilient crops. CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats) technology has emerged as a transformative genome-editing tool due to its efficiency, precision, and ability to generate targeted genetic modifications. This review highlights recent advances in CRISPR genome editing, including base editing, prime editing, and novel Cas variants, together with emerging approaches such as epigenome editing, mitochondrial genome editing, and hypercompact Cas systems, and their applications in improving crop productivity, stress tolerance, and nutritional quality. In food and feed crops, these applications also include crop-specific priorities such as grain and nutritional quality in food crops and digestibility, forage quality, and mineral bioavailability in feed and forage crops. Particular emphasis is placed on the complex intellectual property (IP) landscape surrounding CRISPR technologies, including patents on editing systems, delivery platforms, and proprietary vectors. These intellectual property barriers can restrict research access, technology transfer, and commercialization, particularly in developing countries. The review further discusses patent limitations, licensing frameworks, and strategies to enhance equitable global access through collaborative approaches such as non-exclusive licensing, humanitarian licensing, indigenous technology development, and international partnerships. Overall, the review underscores the need to balance innovation, intellectual property protection, and global accessibility to ensure that CRISPR-based technologies contribute effectively to worldwide food and feed security and sustainable agriculture.
keywords: ['CRISPR-Cas systems', 'Crop improvement', 'Genome editing', 'Global accessibility', 'Intellectual property rights', 'Regulatory frameworks']

title: Advances in plant metabolic engineering through synthetic biology.
authors: ['Hind Alsuwat', 'Derry Alvarez', 'Salim Al-Babili']
abstract: The challenges associated with the escalating global population and climate change in crop production and food security are substantial. This underscores the necessity for improvements in crop nutrition, yield, and resilience to environmental stresses. Plant metabolic pathways directly influence growth, nutrient accumulation, and stress responses, rendering them prime targets for crop enhancement. Advances in plant synthetic biology and gene editing are facilitating more precise modifications of genes, regulatory elements, and metabolic pathways. This review highlights the primary technologies used in plant metabolic engineering and focuses on representative examples of their implementation for crop improvement, including but not limited to CRISPR-Cas systems, multiplex genome editing, knock-in and knock-out strategies, CRISPR-mediated gene regulation (CRISPRi/CRISPRa), base editing, prime editing, RNA targeting technologies, synthetic promoters, and gene stacking strategies. Furthermore, the emerging role of artificial intelligence in the design and optimization of metabolic pathways and genome editing tools will be briefly discussed.
keywords: ['CRISPR', 'genome edited plants', 'plant metabolic engineering', 'plant transformation', 'synthetic biology']

title: Molecular Links Between Heat Stress and DNA Damage Response in Plants.
authors: ['Adrian Calves-Ubach', 'Miriam Szurman-Zubrzycka']
abstract: Climate change poses a major threat to agricultural productivity and, consequently, to global food security. Among the consequences of climate change, heat stress (HS) has emerged as a critical factor limiting crop performance. This has stimulated extensive research over the past decade to elucidate the molecular and physiological mechanisms underlying plant responses to HS. Recent findings indicate that the DNA damage response (DDR) pathway, associated with the maintenance of genome integrity, also plays an important role in plant thermotolerance. This review summarizes recent advances linking DDR components to plant HS responses. We discuss the involvement of the canonical DDR pathway, with particular emphasis on the role of SUPPRESSOR OF GAMMA RESPONSE 1 (SOG1) and its downstream targets in HS responses. In addition, we highlight emerging SOG1-independent modules, including the HOS1-RECQ2 pathway, as well as the recent insights into the plant DREAM complex, which further strengthens the connection between DDR and HS responses. Together, these findings position DDR as a key regulatory node coordinating genome stability, stress signalling and growth modulation under HS conditions. A deeper understanding of this connection may provide new opportunities for developing heat-tolerant crops and improving agricultural resilience in the context of global climate change.

title: Agricultural Landscape Understanding At Country-Scale
authors: ['Radhika Dua', 'Aditi Agarwal', 'Aishwarya Jayagopal', 'Depanshu Sani', 'Alex Wilson', 'Hoang Tran', 'Ishan Deshpande', 'Bogdan Floristean', 'Neelabh Goyal', 'Ramya Cheruvu', 'Vishal Batchu', 'Yan Mayster', 'Gaurav Aggarwal', 'Alok Talekar', 'Vaibhav Rajan']
abstract: Comprehensive agricultural landscape understanding is critical for addressing global challenges in food security, climate change, and resource management. This requires mapping not just crop fields, but also vital features like trees and water bodies which form an intricate mosaic in complex \textit{smallholder} systems dominating the Global South. Previous efforts to develop such land use maps have been limited by a narrow focus on methods for field delineation only, and also do not develop robust post-processing steps essential for real-world deployment. Further, to our knowledge, no prior system for smallholder farms has been deployed and evaluated at a national scale. This work addresses these limitations by presenting the first national-scale agricultural mapping system that moves beyond simple field delineation to enable segmentation of agricultural instances like fields, trees and water bodies. Our system is refined for real-world application using novel post-processing heuristics to ensure map consistency and accuracy, and is validated through a rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation process. Fine-grained land use maps generated by our system are publicly accessible via an API at \textit{\href{http://agri.withgoogle.com}{http://agri.withgoogle.com}}, enabling a wide range of applications from precision agriculture and policy-making to advancing global sustainability development goals.

title: Time series evidence on air quality transitions under urban shock during COVID-19 shutdown in Delhi-NCR, India.
authors: ['Saswati Biswas', 'Samit Bhattacharyya', 'Mudit Yadav', 'Sailesh N Behera', 'Yamini Sistla Sudha']
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic and the associated nationwide lockdown provided an unprecedented natural experiment to investigate how abrupt reductions in anthropogenic activities influence urban air quality. Although several studies have quantified changes in pollutant concentrations during the lockdown, the nonlinear temporal transitions and persistence of these changes after reopening remain poorly understood. This study investigates the evolution of air quality across Delhi-NCR, India, one of the world's most polluted metropolitan regions, by examining three distinct phases associated with the COVID-19 pandemic: the pre-COVID period, the COVID period, and the post-COVID period. Daily concentrations of PM2.5, PM10, NOx, SO2, CO, and O3, together with meteorological observations from ten CAAQMS stations, were analyzed. The analytical framework combined seasonal statistical analysis, ARIMA forecasting, Pearson correlation, principal component analysis, change-point detection, and recurrence quantification analysis to characterize statistical and nonlinear dynamical transitions in air quality. The results reveal significant reductions in pollutant concentrations and pronounced shifts in their temporal dynamics during the lockdown, characterized by multiple change points and altered recurrence structures. Source-related analysis indicates that meteorological factors and secondary pollutant formation played a greater role during the lockdown, whereas combustion and non-combustion emission sources dominated before and after the restrictions. Furthermore, cross-recurrence analysis demonstrates that post-COVID pollutant dynamics remained more synchronized with lockdown conditions than with the pre-COVID period, suggesting partial persistence of environmental improvements. By integrating conventional statistical analyses with nonlinear dynamical systems techniques, this study provides a comprehensive framework for characterizing air-quality transitions and offers policy-relevant insights for sustainable urban air-quality management in rapidly growing megacities.

title: Multidimensional Cardiac Phenotyping of Daphnia magna Enables One-Hour Effect-Based Screening of Aquatic Toxicity.
authors: ['Zitong Liao', 'Zhuo Chen', 'Yun Lu', 'Dongbin Wei', 'Xian-Wei Liu', 'Yinhu Wu', 'Wen-Long Wang', 'Yarong Qi', 'Yuming Wang', 'Ren Ding', 'Hong-Ying Hu']
abstract: Operational water quality management relies on physicochemical monitoring and targeted chemical analysis, but routine surveillance covers only a prioritized subset of high-risk contaminants and does not capture biological activity from unmonitored chemicals, transformation products, or complex mixtures. Whole-organism bioassays provide complementary effect information, yet the conventional Daphnia magna (D. magna) acute immobilization end point requires 48 h. Here, we introduce D-HEART (Daphnia-based Heartbeat Evaluation and Analysis for Rapid Toxicity Screening), a microfluidic imaging and analysis framework that converts high-speed cardiac recordings into 116 descriptors spanning morphology, pumping, wall motion kinematics, and synchrony. Within the tested response space, D-HEART assigns cardiac-response classes using a six-contaminant reference library, while its Heartbeat Toxicity Index (HTI) estimates 48 h immobilization from the predicted class and phenotype. Transcriptomic profiles provided molecular context for differentiated 1 h cardiac states. Post-training Cd(II) tests across environmental water matrices tracked immobilization with greater uncertainty than in laboratory water, and two untreated industrial wastewaters showed dose-responsive HTI estimates for mixed exposures from unseen contaminant classes. By linking early physiological states to transcriptional responses and later apical toxicity, D-HEART provides a rapid, cross-time scale effect-screening layer for operational water-quality evaluation, reducing the detection window by approximately 98% relative to the conventional 48 h immobilization end point.

title: Multidimensional vulnerabilities of informal settlements in the Urban South.
authors: ['Mingxing Chen', 'Wenming Song', 'Dadao Lu', 'Yu Deng', 'Chenglong Wang', 'Huiping Jiang', 'Yuyu Zhou', 'Murray W Scown', 'Liangkan Chen', 'Jing Ma', 'Heran Zheng', 'Xuemei Bai']
abstract: Informal settlements are widespread and rapidly growing, often associated with high vulnerabilities. However, global-scale understanding on their spatial distribution and complexity of vulnerability is limited. Here, we delineate the informal settlements across a sample of 1,914 cities of the Global South by integrating Sentinel-2 imagery with deep learning models, and we explore the heterogeneity of vulnerability using Urban Informal Settlement Vulnerability Index that encompasses living conditions, social infrastructure, and environmental risk. We found that Urban Informal Settlements cover 12.94 ± 2.52% of their total urban areas (approximately 34.04 × 103 km2), especially in sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and Middle Asia. Sub-Saharan African cities have the highest vulnerability of informal settlements, with 31.75 ± 6.20% of total urban areas being occupied by informal settlements, while East Asian cities exhibit relatively low vulnerability across all dimensions. We also find that urban informal settlements with high environmental exposure are widespread in the Global South, and there is a significantly polarized distribution between "low" and "high" vulnerability categories. The findings highlight the disparate distribution of multidimensional vulnerability in informal settlements across the Urban South, providing a comparative evidence base for further local assessment and context-specific policy discussions related to SDG 11.

title: From flood hazard to governable climate risk: An integrated framework for adaptive flood governance and the Flood Resilience and Sustainability Index (FRSI).
authors: ['Ricky Anak Kemarau', 'Siti Norliyana Harun', 'Daniel Ugih Echoh', "Zulfaqar Sa'adi", 'Zaini Sakawi', 'Marlia Mohd Hanafiah', 'Oliver Valentine Eboy', 'Stanley Anak Suab']
abstract: Climate change, urban expansion and ecosystem degradation are intensifying flood-risk management challenges worldwide. However, mitigation and recovery approaches remain fragmented across engineering, community adaptation, technology, governance and finance, limiting integrated assessment of resilience and sustainability. This study examines the reported effectiveness and implementation constraints of flood mitigation and recovery strategies, their integration of sustainability principles, and their implications for adaptive governance. A PRISMA-guided systematic review of 62 studies combines thematic synthesis, comparative framework analysis and semi-quantitative evidence mapping. Strategies are compared across cases using reported effectiveness, implementation cost and complexity, scalability, and sustainability contributions. Standardised evidence-mapping scores support contextual interpretation rather than pooled effect estimates or universal rankings. The synthesis identifies three recurring patterns. First, hybrid approaches combine engineered protection, ecological buffering, early warning and community preparedness, with outcomes dependent on local conditions, maintenance and institutional capacity. Second, fragmented responsibilities, weak enforcement, financing constraints and limited community participation impede implementation and recovery. Third, existing assessment frameworks provide incomplete integration of physical, social, ecological, technological, institutional and financial dimensions. These findings inform the proposed Flood Resilience and Sustainability Index (FRSI), a conceptual framework comprising seven domains: hazard and exposure, vulnerability and equity, infrastructure resilience, ecological and nature-based resilience, governance capacity, technological readiness, and recovery-financial capacity. Its contribution lies in organizing these interdependent domains within a common structure for future resilience assessment and policy prioritization; operationalisation and empirical validation remain necessary. The synthesis supports coordinated institutional responsibilities, enforceable risk-sensitive land-use planning, sustained investment in complementary structural and nature-based measures, and equitable access to preparedness and recovery finance. These priorities connect flood-risk reduction with inclusive recovery and long-term adaptation.
keywords: ['Adaptive flood governance', 'Disaster recovery', 'Flood resilience', 'Flood resilience and sustainability index', 'Nature-based solutions', 'Resilience finance']

title: Trends in Ophthalmic Hospital Transfers and Consultations Across US Academic Centers.
authors: ['Shu Feng', 'Karine D Bojikian', 'Thellea K Leveque', "Jacquelyn O'Banion", 'Daniel B Moore', 'Donna H Kim', 'Andrew T Melson', 'Samuel J Prater', 'Ore-Ofe Adesina', 'Daniel J Ozzello', 'Jeremy Reitinger', 'Ayaka Fujihashi', 'Joseph Bogaard', 'Theresa M Long', 'Manasvee S Kapadia', 'Douglas J Rhee', 'Leona Ding', 'Jennifer T Yu']
abstract: IMPORTANCE: Academic medical centers increasingly serve as a safety net for urgent and complex ophthalmic conditions, yet trends in the demand for hospital-based ophthalmic services remain poorly characterized. OBJECTIVE: To characterize multi-institutional trends in ophthalmology interhospital transfer requests and emergency department (ED) and inpatient ophthalmology consultation requests (hereafter, consultations) from other departments within the same hospital, such as emergency medicine or internal medicine, at multiple academic medical centers in the US. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This retrospective, longitudinal, cohort study involved 14 hospitals affiliated with 10 academic medical centers across multiple geographic regions in the US, representing large urban tertiary referral centers serving diverse catchment populations. Participants were patients for whom ED and inpatient interhospital transfers for ophthalmic care were requested and/or accepted, and patients who received inpatient or ED ophthalmic consultation at participating academic medical centers from 2013 through 2024. EXPOSURE: Participating institutions were required to be academic hospitals with resident participation in on-call coverage and to maintain hospital transfer or consultation data from at least 2017 onward, with the earliest beginning in 2013. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Trends in population-adjusted and hospital volume-adjusted rates of ophthalmology interhospital transfer requests and ED and inpatient ophthalmology consultations. RESULTS: A total of 32 131 ophthalmology transfer requests, 23 560 accepted transfers, and 139 356 ophthalmology consultations (83 581 ED and 44 472 inpatient) were recorded across participating hospitals. Transfer requests increased by an aggregate 0.66 (95% CI, 0.51-0.81) per 100 000 state residents per year and accepted transfers by 0.34 per 100 000 state residents per year (95% CI, 0.17-0.51). Among the 7 institutions with consultation data, consultations increased by an aggregate 3.01 per 100 000 state residents per year (95% CI, 2.33-3.69), comprising 2.06 per 100 000 per year for ED consultations (95% CI, 1.51-2.61) and 1.08 per 100 000 per year for inpatient consultations (95% CI, 0.87-1.30). All aggregate trends were significant (false-discovery rate-adjusted P < .001). CONCLUSIONS: In this cohort study, ophthalmic interhospital transfer requests and inpatient and ED ophthalmology consultations increased substantially across academic medical centers over the study period. These trends suggest growing demand for hospital-based ophthalmic care and increasing strain on ophthalmology hospital coverage, with important implications for workforce sustainability and health system planning.

title: IoT Applications in Urban Sustainability
authors: ['Samiya Khan', 'Mohammad Moazum Wani', 'Mansaf Alam']
abstract: Internet of Things is one of the driving technologies behind the concept of Smart Cities and is capable of playing a significant role in facilitating urban sustainable development. This chapter explores the relationship between three core concepts namely Smart Cities, Internet of Things and Sustainability; thereby identifying the challenges and opportunities that exist in the synergistic use of Internet of Things for sustainability, in the Smart Cities context. Moreover, this chapter also presents some of the existing use cases that apply Internet of Things for urban sustainable development, also presenting the vision for these applications as they continue to evolve in and adapt to the real world scenario. It is because of the interdisciplinary nature of these applications that a clear comprehension of the associated challenges becomes quintessential. Study of challenges and opportunities in this area shall facilitate collaboration between different sectors of urban planning and optimize the utilization of Internet of Things for sustainability.

title: State of the Art Survey of Deep Learning and Machine Learning Models for Smart Cities and Urban Sustainability
authors: ['Saeed Nosratabadi', 'Amir Mosavi', 'Ramin Keivani', 'Sina Ardabili', 'Farshid Aram']
abstract: Deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML) methods have recently contributed to the advancement of models in the various aspects of prediction, planning, and uncertainty analysis of smart cities and urban development. This paper presents the state of the art of DL and ML methods used in this realm. Through a novel taxonomy, the advances in model development and new application domains in urban sustainability and smart cities are presented. Findings reveal that five DL and ML methods have been most applied to address the different aspects of smart cities. These are artificial neural networks; support vector machines; decision trees; ensembles, Bayesians, hybrids, and neuro-fuzzy; and deep learning. It is also disclosed that energy, health, and urban transport are the main domains of smart cities that DL and ML methods contributed in to address their problems.

title: Multivariate Modeling for Sustainable and Resilient Infrastructure Systems and Communities
authors: ['Renee Obringer', 'Roshanak Nateghi']
abstract: Sustainability and resilience of urban systems are multifaceted concepts, requiring information about multiple system attributes to adequately evaluate and characterize. However, despite the scientific consensus on the multivariate nature of these concepts, many of the existing techniques to model urban sustainability and resilience are unidimensional in nature, focusing on a characterizing a single element of highly interconnected urban systems. We champion a paradigm shift in modeling urban sustainability and resilience, using an integrated approach to simultaneously estimate multiple interconnected (correlated) system attributes of sustainability and resilience as a function of key environmental factors. We present a novel case study and review a few recent studies to illustrate the applicability and benefits of the multivariate approach to modeling urban sustainability and resilience. Our proposed framework can be utilized by infrastructure managers, urban planners, and researchers to conceptualize and assess urban sustainability and resilience more holistically, and to better understand the key factors in advancing the sustainability and resilience of infrastructure systems.

title: How are cities pledging net zero? A computational approach to analyzing subnational climate strategies
authors: ['Siddharth Sachdeva', 'Angel Hsu', 'Ian French', 'Elwin Lim']
abstract: Cities have become primary actors on climate change and are increasingly setting goals aimed at net-zero emissions. The rapid proliferation of subnational governments "racing to zero" emissions and articulating their own climate mitigation plans warrants closer examination to understand how these actors intend to meet these goals. The scattered, incomplete and heterogeneous nature of city climate policy documents, however, has made their systemic analysis challenging. We analyze 318 climate action documents from cities that have pledged net-zero targets or joined a transnational climate initiative with this goal using machine learning-based natural language processing (NLP) techniques. We use these approaches to accomplish two primary goals: 1) determine text patterns that predict "ambitious" net-zero targets, where we define an ambitious target as one that encompasses a subnational government's economy-wide emissions; and 2) perform a sectoral analysis to identify patterns and trade-offs in climate action themes (i.e., land-use, industry, buildings, etc.). We find that cities that have defined ambitious climate actions tend to emphasize quantitative metrics and specific high-emitting sectors in their plans, supported by mentions of governance and citizen participation. Cities predominantly emphasize energy-related actions in their plans, particularly in the buildings, transport and heating sectors, but often at the expense of other sectors, including land-use and climate impacts. The method presented in this paper provides a replicable, scalable approach to analyzing climate action plans and a first step towards facilitating cross-city learning.

title: Visual anemometry: physics-informed inference of wind for renewable energy, urban sustainability, and environmental science
authors: ['John O. Dabiri', 'Michael F. Howland', 'Matthew K. Fu', 'Roni H. Goldshmid']
abstract: Accurate measurements of atmospheric flows at meter-scale resolution are essential for a broad range of sustainability applications, including optimal design of wind and solar farms, safe and efficient urban air mobility, monitoring of environmental phenomena such as wildfires and air pollution dispersal, and data assimilation into weather and climate models. Measurement of the relevant microscale wind flows is inherently challenged by the optical transparency of the wind. This review explores new ways in which physics can be leveraged to "see" environmental flows non-intrusively, that is, without the need to place measurement instruments directly in the flows of interest. Specifically, while the wind itself is transparent, its effect can be visually observed in the motion of objects embedded in the environment and subjected to wind -- swaying trees and flapping flags are commonly encountered examples. We describe emerging efforts to accomplish visual anemometry, the task of quantitatively inferring local wind conditions based on the physics of observed flow-structure interactions. Approaches based on first-principles physics as well as data-driven, machine learning methods will be described, and remaining obstacles to fully generalizable visual anemometry will be discussed.

title: Baseline techno-economic and life cycle assessment of black mass production.
authors: ['Tanongsak Yingnakorn', 'Chatisa Kansomket', 'Chaiyasit Longbutsri', 'Sean Scott', 'Tapany Patcharawit', 'Jake M Yang', 'Andrew P Abbott', 'Sakhob Khumkoa']
abstract: Recycling lithium-ion batteries hinges on economically producing black mass-the electrode powder concentrate that feeds downstream metal recovery-yet public baselines pairing real process economics with environmental impacts remain scarce. Here we show that a purely mechanical flowsheet-shredding, zigzag air classification, and circular screen vibration-applied identically to two structurally distinct feedstocks recovers black mass at 93.28 wt % separation efficiency from electric-vehicle modules and 75.77 wt % from mobile phone cells. Built on measured pilot data, loaded processing costs of $0.31-0.73/kg yield net profits of $4.39-5.53/kg under realistic feedstock purchase prices, with a probability of unprofitability below 0.2% across simulated market scenarios. Life cycle assessment attributes most impacts to grid electricity, with a global warming potential of 0.210-0.241 kg CO2 eq./kg input; a low-carbon grid cuts this by 62.8%. This paired baseline enables benchmarking of emerging recycling routes and supports circular battery supply chains.
keywords: ['baseline', 'black mass', 'carbon footprint', 'electric vehicle', 'life cycle assessment', 'lithium-ion batteries', 'mechanical separation', 'techno-economic assessment']

title: Towards a courageous EU policy for recycling spent lithium-ion batteries: rethinking dismantling, standardization, and responsibility.
authors: ['Alessandra Zanoletti', 'Alberto Mannu', 'Gavin D J Harper', 'Elza Bontempi']
abstract: The rapid expansion of electric mobility across Europe is generating, and is expected to generate, unprecedented volumes of end-of-life lithium-ion batteries (LIBs), exposing structural weaknesses in the European Union's regulatory and industrial framework for battery recycling. We have crossed the point at which electric vehicles, for the first time, have out-sold petrol vehicles in Europe. Recent EU initiatives, including the Batteries Regulation, introduce significant advances, including carbon footprint reporting, mandatory recycled content, digital battery passports, sustainability and circularity requirements, and stronger extended producer responsibility. The heterogeneity of battery designs is widely recognized as a key constraint affecting dismantling efficiency, automation feasibility, and material recovery outcomes. These design issues directly impede automation, depress material recovery yields, and undermine the EU's circular economy and industrial sovereignty objectives. Drawing on assertive industrial policies, this paper argues that the EU should adopt a bolder stance. It proposes the introduction of harmonised design-for-disassembly requirements for all batteries placed on the EU internal market, alongside a reform of Extended Producer Responsibility and waste classification to recognise spent batteries as strategic secondary raw materials. It also calls for the development of publicly supported robotised dismantling hubs. The paper argues that the main limitation of current EU battery policy lies not only in downstream recycling performance, but more fundamentally in the absence of binding upstream design requirements that determine whether dismantling, and therefore high-quality recycling, can be technically and economically achieved.

title: Low-frequency non-destructive adaptive fastest pulse preheating for lithium-ion batteries.
authors: ['Chen Li', 'Shuoyuan Mao', 'Ming Gao', 'Mingrui He', 'Yukun Sun', 'Depeng Wang', 'Xuebing Han', 'Cai-Juan Xia', 'Xiaodan Wang', 'Yao Lu', 'Wenchao Gao']
abstract: Low-temperature polarization sharply reduces lithium-ion battery capacity and power, limiting electric vehicles and energy storage systems in cold regions. Bidirectional pulsed current (BPC) self-heating exploits increased internal resistance to enable efficient, rapid, and uniform heating, but high-rate pulses may induce lithium plating. Although high-frequency (>100 Hz) BPC suppresses plating, it requires additional power components. Here, we propose an adaptive, non-destructive BPC heating strategy that adjusts pulse current with temperature and state of charge (SOC), enabling the fastest heating within the lithium-plating-free boundary at low frequencies (<1 Hz). Using parameters optimized with three-electrode cells, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) and nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries were heated from -15°C to 10°C while maintaining the negative electrode potential above 0 V (vs. Li/Li+). After 100 heating cycles, neither chemistry showed capacity degradation, and post-heating analysis revealed no lithium plating, confirming safe and non-destructive low-temperature heating without compromising battery performance or requiring high-frequency auxiliary power electronics.
keywords: ['current pulse', 'heating rate and temperature uniformity', 'lithium-ion battery', 'low temperature heating of lithium-ion battery']

title: Lithium-Borate Interphase Enables High-Rate and Long-Lifespan Ni-Rich Layered Oxide Cathodes.
authors: ['Yu You', 'Shihong Zhao', 'Chen Liu', 'Gang Zhou', 'Xinxin Wang', 'Jian Zhu', 'Chaojiang Niu', 'Chunxiao Zhang', 'Weifeng Wei']
abstract: The growing demand for fast-charging and high-power electric vehicles is shifting Ni-rich cathode design from maximizing energy density alone toward sustaining rapid Li-ion transport over long cycling. LiNixCoyAlzO2 is well suited to this target because its Mn-free, Al-stabilized layered framework offers high capacity and structural robustness, yet residual alkaline lithium species on the particle surface compromise electrode processing, interfacial kinetics and long-term durability. Here we convert these residual lithium species on LiNi0.88Co0.09Al0.03O2 (NCA) surface into a functional lithium-borate interphase through a boric-acid-mediated surface reaction (NCA-B). Rather than simply removing surface residues, this strategy suppresses parasitic interfacial chemistry while maintaining efficient Li-ion transport. In Ah-level NCA-B||graphite pouch cells, the modified cathode retains 76.9% capacity after 2000 cycles at 1 C and sustains nearly decay-free cycling for 2400 cycles under 1 C charge and 10 C discharge, with a voltage-fade rate of 0.0375 mV per cycle. These results establish residual-lithium conversion as a practical interfacial design principle for high-rate, long-life NCA batteries.

title: Battery-type-associated pollutant fingerprints and cytotoxicity of firefighting wastewater from full-scale electric vehicle fires.
authors: ['Qiang Dong', 'Zhan Wang', 'Qi Zhang', 'Yuheng Cheng', 'Huifeng Li', 'Yijia He', 'Xin Zheng', 'Yudie Jianyao', 'Jiale Zhang', 'Yang Yu', 'Guofeng Su', 'Hongyong Yuan', 'Xiaole Zhang']
abstract: The rapid adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) has increased concern over fires, whose suppression generates chemically complex wastewater. However, the temporal evolution and toxicity of EV fire wastewater remain poorly understood. In this study, we conducted full-scale fire and suppression tests on EVs powered by nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, using time-resolved sampling to characterize firefighting runoff and residual wastewater retained after suppression. By integrating chemical profiling and in vitro cytotoxicity assays, we resolved battery-type-associated wastewater hazards. Runoff wastewater exhibited distinct metal-release fingerprints: NMC-runoff carried substantially higher battery-derived ionic loads, with early-stage Li+ reaching 4.26-4.59 mg·L-1, approximately one order of magnitude higher than that in LFP-runoff (averaging 0.36 mg·L-1). Residual pallet wastewater acted as a concentrated pollution reservoir, with NMC samples becoming strongly alkaline (pH>11). Li+ and fluoride in residual wastewater reached about 7.21 × 102 mg·L-1 and 3.85×102 mg·L-1, respectively, generally more than two orders of magnitude higher than in runoff wastewater. Cytotoxicity tests revealed that residual wastewater induced concentration-dependent cytotoxicity, with human neuroblastoma cells being the most sensitive and viability decreasing to 5.7%. These findings identify residual or immersion-type suppression water as a secondary EV fire hazard and support battery-type-specific strategies for emergency management. SYNOPSIS: Full-scale NMC and LFP battery EV fire tests reveal distinct wastewater pollutant fingerprints, sludge properties, and cytotoxic profiles, underscoring the need for chemistry-specific environmental standards and emergency protocols.

title: Autonomous Electric Vehicle Battery Disassembly Based on NeuroSymbolic Computing
authors: ['Hengwei Zhang', 'Hua Yang', 'Haitao Wang', 'Zhigang Wang', 'Shengmin Zhang', 'Ming Chen']
abstract: The booming of electric vehicles demands efficient battery disassembly for recycling to be environment-friendly. Due to the unstructured environment and high uncertainties, battery disassembly is still primarily done by humans, probably assisted by robots. It is highly desirable to design autonomous solutions to improve work efficiency and lower human risks in high voltage and toxic environments. This paper proposes a novel framework of the NeuroSymbolic task and motion planning method to disassemble batteries in an unstructured environment using robots automatically. It enables robots to independently locate and disassemble battery bolts, with or without obstacles. This study not only provides a solution for intelligently disassembling electric vehicle batteries but also verifies its feasibility through a set of test results with the robot accomplishing the disassembly tasks in a complex and dynamic environment.

title: Digital twin and extended reality for teleoperation of the electric vehicle battery disassembly
authors: ['Tero Kaarlela', 'Sami Salo', 'Jose Outeiro']
abstract: Disassembling and sorting Electric Vehicle Batteries (EVBs) supports a sustainable transition to electric vehicles by enabling a closed-loop supply chain. Currently, the manual disassembly process exposes workers to hazards, including electrocution and toxic chemicals. We propose a teleoperated system for the safe disassembly and sorting of EVBs. A human-in-the-loop can create and save disassembly sequences for unknown EVB types, enabling future automation. An RGB camera aligns the physical and digital twins of the EVB, and the digital twin of the robot is based on the Robot Operating System (ROS) middleware. This hybrid approach combines teleoperation and automation to improve safety, adaptability, and efficiency in EVB disassembly and sorting. The economic contribution is realized by reducing labor dependency and increasing throughput in battery recycling. An online pilot study was set up to evaluate the usability of the presented approach, and the results demonstrate the potential as a user-friendly solution.

title: Upcycling Low-Nickel Polycrystalline Cathodes from Retired Electric Vehicle Batteries into Single-Crystal Nickel-Rich Cathodes
authors: ['Guannan Qian', 'Zhiyuan Li', 'Yong Wang', 'Xianyu Xie', 'Yushi He', 'Jizhou Li', 'Yanhua Zhu', 'Zhengjie Chen', 'Sijie Xie', 'Haiying Che', 'Yanbin Shen', 'Liwei Chen', 'Xiaojing Huang', 'Zi-Feng Ma', 'Yijin Liu', 'Linsen Li']
abstract: The electrification revolution in automobile industry and others demands annual production capacity of batteries at least on the order of 102 gigawatts hours, which presents a twofold challenge to supply of key materials such as cobalt and nickel and to recycling when the batteries retire. Pyrometallurgical and hydrometallurgical recycling are currently used in industry but suffer from complexity, high costs, and secondary pollution. Here we report a direct-recycling method in molten salts (MSDR) that is environmentally benign and value-creating based on a techno-economic analysis using real-world data and price information. We also experimentally demonstrate the feasibility of MSDR by upcycling a low-nickel polycrystalline LiNi0.5Mn0.3Co0.2O2 (NMC) cathode material that is widely used in early-year electric vehicles into Ni-rich (Ni > 65%) single-crystal NMCs with increased energy-density (>10% increase) and outstanding electrochemical performance (>94% capacity retention after 500 cycles in pouch-type full cells). This work opens up new opportunities for closed-loop recycling of electric vehicle batteries and manufacturing of next-generation NMC cathode materials.

title: Towards Reuse and Recycling of Lithium-ion Batteries: Tele-robotics for Disassembly of Electric Vehicle Batteries
authors: ['Jamie Hathaway', 'Abdelaziz Shaarawy', 'Cansu Akdeniz', 'Ali Aflakian', 'Rustam Stolkin', 'Alireza Rastegarpanah']
abstract: Disassembly of electric vehicle batteries is a critical stage in recovery, recycling and re-use of high-value battery materials, but is complicated by limited standardisation, design complexity, compounded by uncertainty and safety issues from varying end-of-life condition. Telerobotics presents an avenue for semi-autonomous robotic disassembly that addresses these challenges. However, it is suggested that quality and realism of the user's haptic interactions with the environment is important for precise, contact-rich and safety-critical tasks. To investigate this proposition, we demonstrate the disassembly of a Nissan Leaf 2011 module stack as a basis for a comparative study between a traditional asymmetric haptic-'cobot' master-slave framework and identical master and slave cobots based on task completion time and success rate metrics. We demonstrate across a range of disassembly tasks a time reduction of 22%-57% is achieved using identical cobots, yet this improvement arises chiefly from an expanded workspace and 1:1 positional mapping, and suffers a 10-30% reduction in first attempt success rate. For unbolting and grasping, the realism of force feedback was comparatively less important than directional information encoded in the interaction, however, 1:1 force mapping strengthened environmental tactile cues for vacuum pick-and-place and contact cutting tasks.

title: Hierarchical Bayesian Model for Probabilistic Analysis of Electric Vehicle Battery Degradation
authors: ['Mehdi Jafari', 'Laura E. Brown', 'Lucia Gauchia']
abstract: This paper proposes a hierarchical Bayesian model for probabilistic estimation of the electric vehicle battery capacity fade. Since the battery aging factors such as temperature, current, and state of charge are not fixed, and they change in different times, locations and by the different users, deterministic models with constant parameters cannot accurately evaluate the battery capacity fade. Therefore, a probabilistic presentation of the capacity fade including uncertainties of the measurements or observations of the variables can be a proper solution. We have developed a hierarchical Bayesian Network model for the electric vehicle battery capacity fade considering multiple external variables. The mathematical expression of the model is extracted based on Bayes theorem, the probability distributions for all variables and their dependencies are carefully chosen where the Metropolis Hastings Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling method is applied to generate the posterior distributions. The model is trained with 85 percent of experimental data to obtain its unseen parameters and tested with other 15 percent of data to prove its accuracy. Also, three case studies for different drivers, different grid services frequencies, and different climates are explored to show model flexibility with different input data. The developed model needs training data for parameter tuning in different conditions. However, after training, it has more than 95 percent precision in estimating the battery capacity fade percentage.

title: Next-Generation Frameworks for Hydrogen Production: A Comparative Review of MOFs, COFs, and HOFs.
authors: ['Jehan Y Al-Humaidi', 'Mohammed Muzibur Rahman']
abstract: Hydrogen is a key energy vector in the shift toward carbon-neutral energy systems, such as the global hydrogen economy. Of the possible production pathways, catalytic water splitting (photocatalytic, electrocatalytic, and thermos-catalytic) has drawn particular attention for its potential in producing green hydrogen. Recently, framework materials such as metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), covalent organic frameworks (COFs), and hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) have shown enormous potential as precisely tunable catalytic platforms due to their large surface areas, structural flexibility, and tunable electronic properties. Here, we review MOFs, COFs and HOFs for hydrogen production applications, with a focus on structure-property-performance relationships. MOFs provide a range of metal active sites and porosity, but have low conductivity and low stability in water. COFs, thanks to their extended π-conjugation and strong covalent bonds, have better charge mobility and visible-light absorption, making them promising photocatalysts. While less studied, HOFs offer benefits in terms of their easy preparation and reversible structure but suffer from weak intermolecular forces. We explore the advances in band gap engineering, heterojunction formation, cocatalysts, and defect engineering, in terms of key performance indicators of catalytic activity, including turnover frequency (TOF), quantum efficiency, and overpotential. Finally, key issues such as stability, scalability, and standardization, and emerging trends, including machine learning-aided discovery of materials and integrated solar hydrogen systems, are assessed. Of the three types, COFs and MOF-derived catalysts hold the most promise for scalable green hydrogen generation.

title: Holistic design strategy of ferrocene-based interlayers for ultralow-noise perovskite photodetectors and high-efficiency solar cells.
authors: ['Eunyoung Hong', 'Francesco Vanin', 'William D J Tremlett', 'Patipan Sukpoonprom', 'Shuai Li', 'Qi Liu', 'Somlak Ittisanronnachai', 'Longren Li', 'Zhuoran Qiao', 'Francesco Furlan', 'Davide Nodari', 'Xiao Cheng Zeng', 'Pichaya Pattanasattayavong', 'Artem A Bakulin', 'Nicholas J Long', 'Zonglong Zhu', 'Nicola Gasparini']
abstract: Organometallic ferrocene (Fc)-based interlayers have emerged as effective interfacial modulators for next-generation perovskite optoelectronic devices. The thermally stable Fc core and reversible Fc/Fc+ redox couple, combined with carbonyl linkers, enable strong coordination to halide-related defects and tuneable frontier orbital energies, reducing non-radiative recombination and dark current in perovskite solar cells (PSCs) and perovskite photodetectors (PPDs), respectively. However, previous studies have focused on specific applications separately, resulting in a limited understanding of molecular design principles bridging device operating conditions. Here, we holistically investigate phenyl- and furyl-terminated ester- and ketone-linked Fc interlayers in PSCs and PPDs. By incorporating Fc-derivative interlayers, we demonstrate that the identity of the terminal group critically governs interfacial energetics and thereby directs device performance. Phenyl-based Fc interlayers generate a large potential step at the perovskite surface, as evidenced by a work-function (WF) shift. This creates a localized electrostatic barrier to reverse-biased hole injection, suppressing dark current density (J D) and enhancing the signal-to-noise ratio. In contrast, furyl-based analogs cause a negligible WF shift, leaving the interfacial injection barrier unperturbed. Instead, their illumination-induced band bending promotes balanced charge extraction while passivating surface traps. Electrochemical potential differences associated with ketone- and ester-linkers help explain the respective sub-trends, whereby the former enhance PPD performance, whilst the latter are preferred in photovoltaics. Consequently, PSCs modified with ferrocenyl-bis-furyl-2-carboxylate (F2) achieved state-of-the-art power conversion efficiencies (PCEs), reaching 26.51%, while PPDs modified with ferrocenyl-bis-phenyl-2-ketone (Ph1) attained outstanding specific detectivities, reaching 1.1 × 1013 Jones at -0.5 V (690 nm). These design guidelines highlight the broad applicability of organometallics in perovskite-based optoelectronic devices.

title: Predicting global horizontal irradiance using regression-based machine learning models in high-altitude environments.
authors: ['Milton Edward Humpiri-Flores', 'David Mamani-Pari', 'Danny Lévano', 'Roel Dante Gomez Apaza', 'Esteban Tocto-Cano', 'Ángel Rosendo Condori-Coaquira', 'Javier Linkolk López-Gonzales']
abstract: Global solar radiation is a fundamental component of the Earth's energy balance and plays a critical role in integrating renewable energy into electrical systems. However, its pronounced variability, particularly in high-altitude regions, constrains energy stability and complicates planning processes. This study evaluated regression-based and machine-learning models for 1-day-ahead prediction of global horizontal irradiance (GHI) in Juliaca, Peru (>3,800 m.a.s.l.), using 11 years (2010-2020) of daily NASA POWER data (n = 4,000 observations after cleaning; 80/20 chronological train/test split: training from 2010 to 2018 and testing from 2018 to 2020). During data auditing, we identified that the same-day clearness index (K T ) is algebraically related to the same-day GHI through the extraterrestrial radiation term, which would otherwise inflate the apparent predictive accuracy. Therefore, we restricted same-day predictors to cyclical solar geometry terms and used lagged specific humidity, clearness index, and irradiance values from the previous 1-3 days as legitimate autoregressive information. Under this leakage-free design, Linear Regression achieved the best performance (R 2 = 0.390, MAE = 0.677 kWh m-2d-1, and RMSE = 0.896 kWh m-2d-1), narrowly outperforming gradient boosting (R 2 = 0.384) and polynomial regression (R 2 = 0.381). Random Forest and shallow neural networks followed closely, with all six models exhibiting remarkably comparable performance. Feature-importance and SHAP analyses for the Random Forest model showed that previous-day irradiance and previous-day (lag-1) humidity were the dominant predictors. This pattern may be consistent with short-persistence cloud processes; however, cloud observations are required to verify this interpretation directly. The modest but realistic explanatory power obtained here, together with the diagnostic procedure used to achieve it, offers a template for detecting and avoiding under-reported leakage risk in solar radiation forecasting studies that use clearness-index-derived predictors.
